questions.stem: Does negative feedback prevent changes in the body's internal conditions?

options.text: Yes — negative feedback stops any change from occurring
No — negative feedback allows a change to occur, then reverses it to restore conditions to the set point
Yes — but only for temperature regulation
No — negative feedback amplifies changes

questions.explanation: Negative feedback does NOT prevent changes — it detects a change that has already occurred and then reverses it to bring conditions back to the normal set point. For example, if blood glucose rises, insulin is released to bring it back down. The change must happen first before the body can respond.

questions.stem: Does homeostasis keep internal conditions perfectly constant?

options.text: Yes — conditions are maintained at exactly one value at all times
No — conditions fluctuate around a set point within a narrow range
Yes — but only in healthy individuals
No — conditions change randomly with no pattern

questions.explanation: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within a narrow range around a set point — they are NOT perfectly constant. There is always some fluctuation because the body responds to changes rather than preventing them. Conditions oscillate slightly above and below the set point as negative feedback corrects deviations.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of components in a negative feedback loop?

options.text: Effector → Receptor → Coordinator → Response
Stimulus → Receptor → Coordinator → Effector → Response
Response → Stimulus → Effector → Receptor
Coordinator → Receptor → Stimulus → Effector

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: Stimulus (a change in conditions) → Receptor (detects the change) → Coordinator (processes information, e.g., brain or pancreas) → Effector (muscles or glands that carry out the response) → Response (action that reverses the change).

questions.stem: What is the role of insulin in blood glucose regulation?

options.text: Insulin raises blood glucose levels
Insulin lowers blood glucose levels by stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert glucose to glycogen
Insulin breaks down glycogen into glucose
Insulin has no role in blood glucose control

questions.explanation: Insulin is released by beta cells in the pancreas when blood glucose is HIGH. It lowers blood glucose by: (1) stimulating body cells to take up glucose from the blood, and (2) stimulating the liver to convert glucose into glycogen for storage. Students often confuse insulin (lowers glucose) with glucagon (raises glucose).

questions.stem: What is the role of glucagon?

options.text: Glucagon lowers blood glucose levels
Glucagon raises blood glucose levels by stimulating the liver to convert glycogen back into glucose
Glucagon stores glucose as fat
Glucagon is the same as glycogen

questions.explanation: Glucagon is released by alpha cells in the pancreas when blood glucose is LOW. It raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to break down glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis) and release it into the blood. Note: glucagon (a hormone) and glycogen (a storage polysaccharide) are different things.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?

options.text: There is no difference — they are the same condition
Type 1: the immune system destroys beta cells so no insulin is produced; Type 2: body cells become resistant to insulin or not enough is produced
Type 1 is caused by diet; Type 2 is genetic
Type 1 only affects adults; Type 2 only affects children

questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the body's immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells — no insulin is produced (treated with insulin injections). Type 2 diabetes is where body cells become resistant to insulin or the pancreas produces insufficient insulin — often linked to obesity and lifestyle (treated with diet, exercise, and medication).

questions.stem: Which is an example of positive feedback?

options.text: Blood glucose regulation by insulin
The release of oxytocin during childbirth — contractions stimulate more oxytocin, which increases contractions
Thermoregulation when body temperature rises
The control of breathing rate

questions.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies a change rather than reversing it. During childbirth, uterine contractions cause the release of oxytocin, which stimulates stronger contractions, which causes more oxytocin release — a cycle that continues until birth. Blood clotting is another example. Positive feedback is rare compared to negative feedback.

questions.stem: How does the body respond when core body temperature rises above 37°C?

options.text: Blood vessels constrict, shivering begins, and hairs stand up
Vasodilation occurs (blood vessels near the skin surface widen), sweating increases, and hairs lie flat
The body produces more heat through increased metabolism
No response occurs until temperature reaches 40°C

questions.explanation: When body temperature rises: vasodilation occurs (arterioles near the skin surface widen, increasing blood flow near the surface to lose heat by radiation), sweat glands produce more sweat (which evaporates, cooling the skin), and hairs lie flat (reducing insulating air layer). These are all mechanisms to lose heat.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between nervous and hormonal coordination?

options.text: There is no difference — they work the same way
Nervous responses are fast, short-lived, and targeted; hormonal responses are slower, longer-lasting, and more widespread
Nervous responses use hormones; hormonal responses use electrical impulses
Only the nervous system is involved in homeostasis

questions.explanation: Nervous responses: travel as electrical impulses along neurones, very fast, short-lived, precise/targeted. Hormonal responses: travel as chemicals in the blood, slower, longer-lasting, affect multiple target organs. Both systems work together to coordinate body functions and maintain homeostasis.

options.text: No — set points are always fixed and never change
Yes — for example, during a fever, the temperature set point is raised by the hypothalamus
No — but the range of fluctuation can increase
Yes — but only the blood glucose set point

questions.explanation: Set points can change. During a fever, pyrogens (chemicals released during infection) cause the hypothalamus to raise the temperature set point. The body then uses normal thermoregulatory mechanisms (shivering, vasoconstriction) to reach this new, higher set point. When the infection clears, the set point returns to normal.
